title: Cross-Document Event Coreference Resolution on Discourse Structure
research_question: Does representing global discourse structure and long-distance discourse paths improve clustering of event mentions across documents that refer to the same real-world event?
methodology: The model combines a local event-pair representation from pretrained language-model embeddings with a global representation derived from rhetorical discourse trees. For cross-document pairs, the authors construct combined discourse structures, extract lowest-common-parent information and shortest dependency paths between discourse units, encode path information with a BiLSTM, and feed local and global representations to an MLP pairwise classifier followed by best-first clustering. Experiments use the standard ECB+ train/dev/test split with gold event mentions and evaluate MUC, B3, CEAFe, and aggregate CoNLL scores against prior CD-ECR systems, with ablations isolating within-document global features, cross-document global features, discourse paths, and tree-construction strategies.

key_findings.finding: The task explicitly defines cross-document event identity as grouping event mentions from different documents that refer to the same real-world event.

Adding within-document discourse lowest-common-parent information raised CoNLL from 81.1 to 82.3, adding cross-document LCP information raised it further to 83.9, and adding discourse-tree shortest-path information raised it to 85.7.
The ablation results provide direct evidence that cross-document global discourse information contributes beyond local event-sentence representations when deciding event identity.
With Longformer as encoder, the proposed model reached a CoNLL score of 86.4 and significantly exceeded the strongest reported comparison by 0.7 points.

The best cross-document discourse construction strategy retained the event sentences while compressing other context; using only event sentences lost useful contextual links, while concatenating full documents introduced excessive noise.
key_findings.section: Analysis on Construction Strategy for Cross Document Discourse Structure

key_findings.finding: A case analysis shows that discourse paths can propagate a shared participant across differing local descriptions and thereby recover coreference that direct local comparison would misclassify.
The study directly addresses cross-document event identity but uses news articles rather than enterprise emails or chats, so workplace continuity remains untested.

limitations: Training and evaluation use gold event mentions, so upstream event-detection errors are excluded.
The discourse-structure constructor has high inference cost.
The authors state that cross-document discourse-tree construction remains open to further optimization.
Evaluation is limited to ECB+, a news-domain benchmark.
The pipeline first clusters documents to topics and only considers mention pairs within the same document cluster, so topic-prediction errors can constrain later coreference decisions.
The work evaluates binary full coreference, not partial or evolving-event relations such as subevent identity.
No enterprise email, workplace chat, ticket, or business-process corpus is evaluated.
No code release is stated in the paper.
raw_claims: Cross-document event coreference clusters mentions from different documents that denote the same real-world event.
The proposed architecture combines local event representations with global discourse-tree representations.
Cross-document lowest-common-parent information improves performance beyond within-document discourse information.
Shortest paths through the discourse tree add further information about long-distance event interactions.
The RoBERTa local-only baseline has a CoNLL score of 81.1 in the reported ablation.
The complete RoBERTa discourse model reaches 85.7 CoNLL in that ablation.
The Longformer version reaches 86.4 CoNLL in the main comparison.
Event-sentence-plus-compressed-context discourse trees outperform event-sentence-only and full-document alternatives.
Full-document tree construction introduces distracting information.
The model is evaluated with annotated event mentions rather than predicted mentions.
The discourse constructor is computationally expensive.
The study uses ECB+ news documents rather than enterprise communications.
